q-162577.name: Question 1
q-162577.problem:
Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=0,$ $x=3,$ $y=-1,$ $y=2,$ $z=0,$ $z=4.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $F=y{e}^{x}\,i+{z}^{2}\,j+3z\,k,$ the flux of $F$ across $S$ can be written as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4}\,\bbox[2pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAA}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

What is the missing part of the expression?
q-162577.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{x})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(3z) \\  & =y{e}^{x}+0+3 \\  & =y{e}^{x}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}(y{e}^{x}+3)\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4}\,y{e}^{x}+3\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{z}^{3})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xz) \\  & =0+0+x \\  & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}x\,\text{d}V,
$$

where $R$ is a type II solid region that can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le y\le 1,\,0\le z\le 2,\,y-z\le x\le 1+{y}^{2}\}.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}x\,\text{d}V & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y-z}^{1+{y}^{2}}\,x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xz)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(y) \\  & ={y}^{2}+0+0 \\  & ={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V,
$$

where $R$ is a type II solid region that can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le y\le 1,\,0\le z\le 1,\,y-2z\le x\le 4-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}\}.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y-2z}^{4-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}}\,{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

q-162588.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}z) \\  & =1+(-2)+{x}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}({x}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}V,
$$

where $R$ is a type I solid region that can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1,\,y\le z\le {x}^{2}+y\}.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}-1\,\text{d}V & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{{x}^{2}+y}\,{x}^{2}-1\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

∬SF⋅dS=∭RdivFdV.

divF=∂∂x(x+y)+∂∂y(−2y)+∂∂z(x2z)=1+(−2)+x2=x2−1.

∬SF⋅dS=∭R(x2−1)dV,

q-162578.problem: Consider the positively (outward) oriented surface $S$ given by ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+(z-4)^{2}=4$ and the vector field $F=z\,i+6y\,j+(x+3z)\,k.$ Use the divergence theorem to find the flux of $F$ across $S.$
q-162578.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x+3z) \\  & =0+6+3 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid sphere of radius $2$ enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}9\,\text{d}V \\  & =9{∭}_{R}\,\text{d}V \\  & =9\cdot \text{Volume}(R) \\  & =9\cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi \cdot {2}^{3} \\  & =96\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

q-162411.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+y) \\  & =0+2+0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}2\,\text{d}V \\  & =2{∭}_{R}\,\text{d}V \\  & =2\cdot \text{Volume}(R) \\  & =2\cdot \pi \cdot {1}^{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
